title: Supernovae & Neutron Stars
hook: When a giant star dies, its core collapses and its outer layers blast away in a supernova that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy — leaving behind something extraordinary.
key_points: A massive star's core collapses when it runs out of fuel, triggering a supernova.
The explosion can briefly outshine a whole galaxy and scatter heavy elements.
What remains is often a neutron star — a teaspoon of it weighs billions of tons.
The most massive stars leave a black hole instead.
content_html: A massive star spends its life fending off gravity with the energy of fusion. When the fuel finally runs out, gravity wins all at once: the core collapses in a fraction of a second, and the rebound blows the star's outer layers into space in a supernova. For a few weeks the explosion can shine as brightly as billions of stars combined.
extra_html: Supernovae are also cosmic factories, flinging the heavy elements made inside the star out into the galaxy. The collapsed core left behind is often a neutron star — matter crushed so hard that a single teaspoon would weigh billions of tons. If the original star was massive enough, gravity doesn't stop there and the core becomes a black hole instead. Wikipedia covers the kinds of supernovae and the exotic remnants they leave.

related.title: The Life Cycle of Stars
related.hook: Stars are born in collapsing gas clouds, spend their lives fusing hydrogen into helium, then die in ways that depend entirely on how heavy they are.

related.title: Black Holes
related.hook: A black hole is a place where gravity wins so completely that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the edge called the event horizon.

related.title: The Amaterasu Particle Might Not Be a Proton
related.hook: One of the most energetic cosmic rays ever caught hit Earth with the energy of a thrown brick — packed into a single particle. New work says it may be a heavy nucleus, not a proton.

related.title: A Galaxy That Makes Neutrinos Without a Black Hole
related.hook: Astronomers expected a feeding black hole behind a flood of cosmic neutrinos. Instead they found furious star formation — hinting dusty starburst galaxies seed the high-energy neutrino sky.

related.title: A Supernova That Peeled Back a Star's Layers
related.hook: A rare supernova exposed material from one of the deepest layers of a dying star — a direct look inside the element factory hidden in massive stars.

flashcards.prompt: What triggers a supernova in a massive star?
flashcards.back_html: Its core collapses once it runs out of fuel, and the outer layers blast away in a colossal explosion.

flashcards.prompt: What is left behind after many supernovae?

choices.text: An ultra-dense neutron star (or a black hole for the biggest stars)
A cloud of cold hydrogen and nothing else

flashcards.explanation_html: The collapsed core can become a neutron star, or for the most massive stars, a black hole.

flashcards.prompt: How dense is a neutron star?

choices.text: So dense that a teaspoon would weigh billions of tons
About the same density as ordinary rock

flashcards.explanation_html: Neutron stars pack a star's worth of mass into a city-sized ball, making them almost unimaginably dense.
